title: Ryan, LLC v. Federal Trade Commission
lead: The Federal Trade Commission’s nationwide noncompete rule drew a statutory and administrative-law challenge. The district court moved from party-limited preliminary relief to a nationwide merits order setting the rule aside.

actors.name: Business association intervenors
actors.role: United States Chamber of Commerce, Business Roundtable, Texas Association of Business, and Longview Chamber of Commerce

proceedings: Ryan sued April 23, 2024 and amended May 1.
July 3 preliminary protection covered only Ryan and named intervenors.
August 20 cross-motion decision set rule aside nationwide.
limits: Court decided statutory authority and arbitrary-and-capricious grounds, reserving remaining constitutional and other theories. Later appeal dismissal and regulatory removal are separate developments reported in assigned material, not a new current-law audit.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The Commission adopts a broad employment rule
paragraphs: The Federal Trade Commission adopted its Non-Compete Clause Rule in April 2024. It treated entering or enforcing most employment noncompetes as unfair competition. It barred new agreements even for qualifying senior executives while preserving their existing agreements; for other covered workers it also reached existing restraints. Exceptions covered bona fide business sales, previously accrued claims, and certain good-faith beliefs that the rule did not apply. It displaced state permission for prohibited agreements while preserving parallel restrictions and enforcement. September 4 was the scheduled effective date.

Ryan, LLC sued April 23 and amended May 1 under the Administrative Procedure Act and Declaratory Judgment Act. The United States Chamber of Commerce, Business Roundtable, Texas Association of Business, and Longview Chamber of Commerce intervened as plaintiffs. On July 3, Judge Ada Brown granted preliminary protection only to Ryan and those intervenors, finding likely statutory overreach, likely arbitrary decisionmaking, and irreparable injury.

sections.title: The parties seek a merits decision
sections.cue: Which arguments the court actually reaches
paragraphs: Plaintiffs moved for summary judgment July 19; the Commission cross-moved August 2. Ryan challenged delegated authority, unconstitutional delegation, retroactivity, decisionmaking, and protections insulating commissioners from presidential control. The associations also challenged the meaning of unfair competition, categorical breadth, alternatives, and cost-benefit analysis. The Commission defended congressional authorization for rulemaking and adjudication, its competition mission, the delegation’s guiding principle, and the record, while disputing the remaining objections.

The court independently examined each cross-motion rather than assuming they eliminated factual disputes. Under the Administrative Procedure Act it resolved statutory authority independently, citing the Supreme Court’s Loper Bright decision rejecting Chevron deference, and reviewed the agency’s stated reasons. It found two sufficient grounds: lack of statutory authority and arbitrary and capricious action. It expressly did not decide the remaining arguments, including removal protections or every delegation challenge.

sections.title: Section 6(g) does not supply the asserted legislative power
paragraphs: Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act provided administrative proceedings and cease-and-desist orders against unfair competition. Section 6 listed mainly investigative and ministerial powers; subsection (g) allowed corporate classification and rules carrying out the subchapter. Brown recognized some rulemaking authority, including competition-related authority, but distinguished procedural rules from legislative rules independently imposing binding duties.

The claimed power appeared within the seventh of twelve mostly investigative provisions, alongside corporate classification, without express reference to section 5’s substantive standard or penalties for rule violations. In the court’s view, that placement and absence of sanctions contrasted with substantive adjudicatory orders and indicated housekeeping power.

The Commission had disclaimed substantive rulemaking for forty-eight years before asserting it in 1962. The D.C. Circuit’s National Petroleum Refiners decision later approved that assertion, but Brown declined its interpretation. Subsequent express grants for particular subjects and for unfair or deceptive practices showed Congress knew how to confer binding power. Preserving any competition-rulemaking authority in the 1975 amendments did not affirmatively create it, nor did unchanged language and definitions in the 1980 amendments establish ratification.

sections.title: Breadth and unexplained alternatives supply a separate defect
paragraphs: Even under deferential review, the Commission had to connect its evidence to the chosen policy. Brown found no adequate bridge from studies of varied state restrictions to a nearly universal, indefinite nationwide prohibition. She criticized inconsistent evidence, overlooked benefits and contrary evidence, and the failure to explain why harmful categories could not be targeted. This did not declare every individual noncompete fair or enforceable.

The Commission also insufficiently addressed reliance and alternatives. Concerns about case-by-case enforcement and assertions that employers could use other protections did not adequately justify rejecting less disruptive distinctions or exceptions. The court’s criticism concerned the agency’s actual explanation, not authority for judicial policy substitution.

On August 20 the court granted plaintiffs’ motions, denied the Commission’s, and set the rule aside under the Administrative Procedure Act. Applying Fifth Circuit remedial precedent, it rejected party-limited final relief: the rule could not take effect September 4 or thereafter nationwide. The assigned later regulatory account separately reports that the Commission dismissed its Ryan and Properties appeals in September 2025, accepted vacatur, and removed the regulation in a February 2026 notice. Those developments followed the 2024 merits decision.
